item.title: Physicists prove a long-suspected quantum speed limit for thermalization
item.description: Whether we are waiting for a car windshield to defrost in winter or a warm drink to cool down, how long it takes for an object to settle into a stable, even temperature within its environment (thermal equilibrium) depends on numerous factors. These can include surface area, the material properties of an object and airflow.

item.title: Laser pulses bring order to a quantum material's tiny electrical regions
item.description: Physicists at Auburn University have used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged "islands" inside a crystal. The discovery helps answer a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows how light could be used to control its behavior—a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information.

item.title: A new way to detect stabilizing properties of optical devices
item.description: In optical fibers, chips and other light-guiding devices, minor defects can scatter photons and disrupt their path. A new study demonstrates a way to reveal properties which, in certain systems, help light wave behavior withstand such flaws. The method could help speed up the search for new kinds of electronics and optical technologies, and contribute to more reliable quantum devices.

item.title: A highway instead of a racetrack: Strong coupling of light and sound in an optical fiber
item.description: For the first time, scientists have achieved strong coupling between light and long-lived acoustic vibrations in an optical fiber. Optical fibers are used in both classical telecommunications and quantum communication and could serve not only as connections between computing nodes but also as quantum processors themselves in the future. The results, published in Nature Physics, pave the way for new technologies in quantum signal processing.

item.title: Quantum calculations reveal how spin defects lose energy
item.description: When light hits a tiny defect embedded in a solid material like diamond or silicon carbide, it can kick the defect's electrons into an excited state. These spin defects have the potential to be used as stable, readable qubits for quantum technologies, for example, quantum sensing. But modeling the full physics of their energetics over time—a key step in developing spin defects into new technologies—is a challenging task.

item.title: New framework links magnetic phase boundaries to string-like defects in spin ice
item.description: A research team led by Haruki Watanabe, a professor in the Department of Physics and the Jockey Club Institute for Advanced Study (IAS) at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), in collaboration with professor Yukitoshi Motome and graduate student Sena Watanabe from the University of Tokyo, has developed a unified theory that predicts when two states of matter are genuinely distinct and when they are actually the same.

item.title: 诺奖颁给冰立方：“天马行空的想法，值得被支持几十年”
item.description: 2026年10月6日，冰立方中微子天文台（IceCube）项目发起人弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）获得诺贝尔物理学奖。

item.title: “冰立方”为何获得2026诺贝尔物理奖？现场对话诺奖评委
item.description: 1988年，弗朗西斯·哈尔岑（Francis Halzen）提出一个构想，利用南极深处的冰层探测来自宇宙的中微子。二十多年后，这一构想成为覆盖一立方公里冰层的冰立方（IceCube）中微子天文台。借助埋在冰中的光传感器，研究人员捕捉到了具有天体物理起源的高能中微子，为研究遥远宇宙中的高能过程提供了新的观测途径。

item.title: Quantum sensor could measure how Earth drags spacetime
item.description: Einstein's theory of general relativity describes gravity as the bending of spacetime, a mathematical model that combines three-dimensional space and time into a single, four-dimensional continuum. The theory also predicts that a rotating object, such as Earth, slightly drags the surrounding spacetime as it rotates, a phenomenon known as frame-dragging.

item.title: 2026诺贝尔化学奖给了法国95岁学者和日本75岁学者，日本科学诺奖得主已有28位
item.description: 10月7日，2026年诺贝尔化学奖授予亨利·卡根（Henri B. Kagan）和硤合宪三（Kenso Soai），以表彰他们“发现不对称有机合成中的非线性效应与自催化现象”。2001年，诺贝尔化学奖表彰不对称催化研究，获奖者为威廉·诺尔斯、野依良治和巴里·夏普莱斯。卡根未获奖，引发法国学界不满，时任法国科研部长致信诺贝尔基金会。《自然》当年报道了这场争议。25年后，95岁的卡根因不对称合成中另一项贡献终获诺奖。

item.title: X-rays reveal surprisingly long-lived spin waves in copper oxide
item.description: Today's computer technology, based on silicon chips, is slowly reaching its physical limits. Components cannot be miniaturized indefinitely, and clock speeds cannot be increased indefinitely. At the same time, huge AI data centers are being built in many places, and these consume an immense amount of electricity. This is why scientists around the world are searching for novel materials that can replace or complement silicon technology and consume significantly less electricity.

item.title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?
item.description: Unlike other recent AI proofs, this one has been unpacked by human experts. The implications, one mathematician said, are “staggering.” The post AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Hybrid diamond chip strengthens interactions between light and quantum bits
item.description: Researchers have developed and demonstrated a new hybrid photonic platform that integrates quantum emitters with photonic devices, providing a way to reliably control the interaction between photons and quantum information carriers. The chip-based platform, which combines gallium phosphide (GaP) with a diamond substrate, could help make quantum networks more practical by providing a way to connect quantum devices over long distances.

item.title: Quantum magic state cleanup cuts errors 40-fold in first successful hardware test
item.description: Qubits, the quantum equivalent of digital bits, are fragile and prone to errors. That makes building reliable quantum computers extremely difficult. One fix has been to use traditional magic state distillation, which filters out flaws, but it is extremely resource-intensive.

item.title: New high-frequency method boosts 2D material readout for next-gen quantum computers
item.description: Quantum computers represent a next step in the fast-paced evolution of technology. Using quantum bits (qubits), they have the potential to run certain calculations exponentially faster than conventional computers. However, developing and fine-tuning quantum computers requires an enormous number of repetitive tests. To accelerate quantum technology development, we need a method that can read quantum states at ultrafast speeds.

item.title: Infrared light overcomes mirror coating obstacle in gravitational wave detector upgrades
item.description: Researchers have developed and tested a new locking method for gravitational wave detectors that will advance the discovery of distant black holes and neutron stars colliding.

item.title: World-record intensity in attosecond hard-X-ray pulses could unlock closer study of electrons in atoms and molecules
item.description: Researchers used the European XFEL to create X-ray flashes that were not only extremely short but also reached record intensity for this type of pulse. The researchers focused the X-rays to an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross section of a typical human hair. This concentrated the X-ray light into a tiny but extremely powerful spot. The method could enable detailed studies of how electrons behave in atoms and molecules and, in the long term, could even allow researchers to contro

item.title: Maxwell's demon learns to turn concealed information into usable energy for microscopic systems
item.description: Since its introduction more than 150 years ago, the thought-provoking idea of Maxwell's demon has profoundly shaped our understanding of the relationship between information and energy. Maxwell's demon is an imagined microscopic gatekeeper that exploits information at the microscopic scale to produce macroscopic work.

item.title: Physics-guided AI reconstructs hidden patterns inside ultrathin magnets from external fields
item.description: To build faster and more energy-efficient computers, researchers need to understand nanoscale magnetic materials. But looking inside these tiny magnets is surprisingly difficult: Modern microscopes only measure the magnetic field outside the material, not the magnetic pattern inside. Because many different internal patterns can produce the exact same field, working backwards has long been a challenge.

item.title: Even or odd numbers: A single molecule makes all the difference in the quantum world
item.description: The researchers in the Quantum Detection Microscopy group at CIC nanoGUNE, in collaboration with chemists at CiQUS of the University of Santiago de Compostela, have demonstrated that adding or removing a single molecule from a quantum chain can fundamentally change its interaction with a superconductor.

item.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
item.description: Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable. The post He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Scientists have just voted to abolish leap seconds
item.description: Since 1972, officials have added 27 leap seconds to the universal clock, but in a meeting this week in France they have decided to abandon the practice

item.title: Will physics be the next field to be turned upside down by AI?
item.description: AI has taken huge strides in computer programming and mathematics – physics could be next

item.title: New spectroscopy method enables direct comparisons of nuclear sizes across heavy elements
item.description: The size of a nucleus (nuclear charge radius) is an important physical quantity that reflects the arrangement of protons and neutrons within the nucleus. Particularly in deformed nuclei, such as those of rare-earth elements, examining changes in the charge radius can deepen our understanding of nuclear structure and nuclear deformation.

item.title: New chip-scale gyroscope measures rotation with unprecedented sensitivity
item.description: Researchers have developed a chip-scale optical ring-laser gyroscope that can measure rotation as slow as 37 degrees per hour. This record sensitivity, approaching Earth's rotation rate of 15 degrees per hour, could eventually be useful for precision navigation and orientation systems, particularly where GPS is unavailable.

item.title: Software advance brings complex quantum simulations to standard computers
item.description: A major software advance could aid the creation of bigger, more reliable quantum computers, a study suggests. Researchers have developed an algorithm that enables off-the-shelf computers to run quantum simulations previously only possible using the world's most powerful supercomputers.

item.title: A tiny magnetic whirlpool could point to a new kind of ultra-efficient memory
item.description: Every time a computer stores or erases information, it uses energy. The amount is tiny for a single operation, but those operations happen billions of times every second. For decades, scientists have wondered just how little energy a memory device could use before reaching the fundamental theoretical limit set by the laws of physics. Now, researchers have shown that it is possible to come close.

item.title: 光遗传学终于获得诺奖
item.description: 2026年10月5日，诺贝尔大会宣布，2026年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖授予卡尔·戴瑟罗斯（Karl Deisseroth）、彼得·黑格曼（Peter Hegemann）和格奥尔格·纳格尔（Georg Nagel），以表彰他们“在光门控离子通道和光遗传学方面的发现”。

item.title: 杨振宁先生在石溪
item.description: 对于杨振宁，中国读者熟悉的，多是他2003年回到清华园之后的岁月；而从1966年至1999年在石溪的33年，是杨振宁一生中最长的一段任职。

item.title: 诺奖得主格拉肖忆杨振宁：“我依然认为他是天才”
item.description: 诺奖得主格拉肖眼中的杨振宁：敢发表“错”论文的天才。
